newsitem.title: USA: Stocks soar as Fed keeps hands off interest rates.
newsitem.headline: Stocks soar as Fed keeps hands off interest rates.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks jumped Tuesday, lifting the Dow Jones industrial average within a few points of a record close as Wall Street welcomed the Federal Reserve's decision to keep interest rates unchanged.

The Dow, which spent most of the session mired in the minus column, exploded in mid-afternoon trading to end with a gain of 74.58 points, or 1.03 percent, at 7,303.46. This was just short of last Thursday's record finish of 7,333.55.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,410 to 1,042 on moderately active volume of 447 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index jumped 22.64 points, or 1.69 percent, to 1,363.88 amid big gains in technology stocks.

News of the Fed's decision brought some immediate relief. Beforehand, Wall Street analysts were sharply divided over whether the central bank would raise interest rates, with a slim majority polled by Reuters ahead of Tuesday's meeting expecting policy-makers to stand pat.
"It's good for the market short-term ... but it leaves some uncertainty about what the Fed is going to do long-term," said Pierre Ellis, senior economist at Primark Decision Economics.

That leaves a "cloud over the market," he said. "We can't really tell what (the Fed) thinks, which means the markets will ... be back to watching data piece by piece" for clues to whether it will take action at its next policy making-meeting on July 1-2.
"That's a guaranteed recipe for volatility", said Harris Bank/Bank of Montreal's chief economist Tim O'Neill, as the market gyrates with every piece of incoming economic data.

The bond market also was higher, with the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond up 7/32, or $2.19 per $1,000 face value, which lowered its yield to 6.90 percent from 6.92 percent at Monday's close. Prices and yields move in opposite directions.

"There's clear-cut evidence the economy is slowing with no inflation around right now," said Martin Regalia, chief economist at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. "To have raised rates on the anticipation of inflation would have been extremely myopic."
Fed officials have cited wage pressures as a harbinger of inflation, but business and labour economists say the job market still has ample slack to supply workers at prevailing wages.

At its last meeting in March, the inflation-wary Fed raised the key federal funds rate -- the rate commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans -- by one quarter percentage point. It was the first increase in more than two years.

Recent data has shown that inflation is not a threat. The Producer Price Index tumbled 0.6 percent in April, its biggest drop in nearly four years, while the Consumer Price Index rose just 0.1 percent.

"The market still confronts a dilemma. Only a steady deceleration in the U.S. economy would prevent the Fed from a July tightening and that means earnings disappointments," said Doug Cliggott, U.S. equity strategist at J.P. Morgan.
"On the other hand, if the economy picks up over the summer, the Fed comes back into play because we might need a tightening," he added.

Banking stocks, which were hurt by fears of an interest rate hike, roared. J.P. Morgan & Co. Inc. jumped 2-3/4 to 105-1/4. Chase Manhattan Corp. added 3-7/8 to 96-1/4, Citicorp rose 3-5/8 to 119-5/8 and First Union Corp. was up 2-7/8 to 87-1/8.
Semiconductor stocks rode a wave of optimism after Merrill Lynch said it expected Intel's revenue growth to rise to 36 percent annually from 30 percent annually, traders said.
Intel surged 6-1/4 to 161. Applied Materials Inc. rose 3-3/16 to 69-15/16 and Altera Corp. jumped 3-1/8 to 51-1/2.
C-Cube Microsystems Inc. fell 5-5/8 to 19-7/8 after it warned that its second quarter earnings would be worse than expected.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 8.39 points to 841.66. The American Stock Exchange index rose 3.28 to 590.76.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 3.06 to 437.20. The average share was up 30 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was at a record high of 7,927.227 up 66.16 or 0.84 percent.
